extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and patent prosecutors (attorneys, agents preparing and prosecuting US patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting specifications and claim sets and for arguing before examiners/PTAB to limit or defeat overly broad constructions under the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) used in USPTO prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: CLEARLY DEFINE CLAIM TERMS IN THE SPECIFICATION
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may be his or her 'own lexicographer and/or may disavow claim scope,' but to do so, the 'patentee must clearly express that intent in the written description.' M.P.E.P. § 2111. Explicit definitions in the specification can be used strategically to assign a special (narrow) definition that avoids known prior art or excludes an inapplicable plain-and-ordinary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although drafters often avoid explicit definitions to evade unnecessarily limiting claims, in appropriate situations lexicography should be used to define terms narrowly. The specification is the single best guide to claim meaning (see Abbott). Even where not in definitional format, the specification may define terms by implication (see In re Chaganti; In re Suitco Surface). Anti-pattern: omitting definitions and thereby allowing claim terms to be construed more broadly under BRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: USE TERMS TO EXPLAIN THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN CLAIM ELEMENTS
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting claims, use language (antecedent basis, relative terms like 'other') to show that different claim elements refer to distinct items and to prevent improper conflation of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate use of antecedent basis and relative terms can demonstrate that elements are separate and should not be merged by an examiner. Example: Microsoft Corp. v. Proxyconn — 'two other computers' recited independently plus the word 'other' denotes a further level of distinction, undermining an interpretation that collapses those computers into the caching computer. Draft claims to make relationships explicit to avoid unreasonable constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: RELY ON SPECIFICATION TO LIMIT REACH OF BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent explicit definitions, read claim language in light of the specification as one of ordinary skill would; the specification often provides the best ammunition against an unreasonable, overly broad PTO construction under BRI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument strategy: point to specification teachings, embodiments, and contextual language (including non-exhaustive lists or phrasing that shows boundaries) to show that a proposed broad construction is unreasonable. Cases: In re Abbott Diabetes Care (spec read in light of specification), In re Chaganti (specification undermined PTAB interpretation). Note that terms defined by implication in the spec can defeat PTO constructions that include features contrary to the spec's embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: CITE OTHER CLAIM LIMITATIONS TO SHOW A PROFFERED CONSTRUCTION IS ILLOGICAL
rubrics_metrics.description: Use other express claim limitations to demonstrate that an overly broad construction would create illogical results or render other claim limitations redundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that construing a term to include features already recited elsewhere makes those recitations redundant (Apple v. Ameranth). Use the claim's full language and clauses to demonstrate that the examiner/PTAB construction conflicts with how the claim reads (D'Agostino example regarding 'single merchant'). Examples include PPC Broadband (continuity member language) and D'Agostino. Strategy: point to internal claim structure and express recitations to argue unreasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: USE DEPENDENT CLAIMS AND CLAIM DIFFERENTIATION TO GIVE FURTHER CONTEXT
rubrics_metrics.description: Include dependent claims that add features or restrictive language to provide fallback positions and to guide interpretation of terms in independent claims via the doctrine of claim differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims can (a) create fallback claim scope and (b) set inner boundaries for terms in independent claims because if a proposed construction of an independent claim would nullify dependent claims, claim differentiation creates a presumption that such a construction is improper (Marine Polymer Techs. v. HemCon). Draft dependent claims intentionally to provide contextual anchoring against broad BRI constructions.
